\label{ch:usar-y-tocar}
\hlchaptermodality{385}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say usar, tocar, mezclar and colgar, and name four everyday actions.}

\section[usar]{usar — a word English has, without knowing it}

\label{lesson:ES-C385-usar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to die}, then \emph{to forget}. (\emph{Morir}; \emph{olvidar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la llave — something you use.
  \item la mano — what you use it with.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{u-SAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{s} sits between two vowels and stays a clean hiss — never a buzz. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{usar} — \textquotedblleft{}to use.\textquotedblright{}

English has this verb already. Not a relative of it: the same verb. Spoken Latin made \textbf{usare} out of \emph{uti}, to use, and \emph{usare} went two ways at once — south into Spanish as \emph{usar}, north through French into English as \textbf{use}.

One thing to notice about that \emph{usare}, because it is a habit worth building. It is printed with a \textbf{star} in front of it, and the star means \emph{reconstructed}: no Roman text from the period that matters here uses the word. Scholars worked backwards from the words that survive. (It does turn up in much later legal Latin, in charters of the eight-hundreds — but by then Romance was already forming, so those are not evidence for the earlier stage.) The Academy's dictionary prints no origin for \emph{usar} at all; a starred ancestor is not the kind of thing it lists. Corominas supplies it, star and all.

So the interesting part is not the meaning. It is the three English words built on the same Latin that no longer look like using anything.

\textbf{Usury} is the plainest of them. It meant payment for the \emph{use} of money, and that is all it meant — a use, a usage. There was no accusation in the word. The disapproval arrived later and stuck so hard that the neutral sense is gone.

A \textbf{utensil} is, word for word, \emph{something that is to be used}. Any tool at all, in Latin. English shrank it down to a kitchen drawer.

And \textbf{abuse} is \emph{ab-} on the front of \emph{uti}: to use \emph{away}, to use something up. The Latin describes a direction, not a crime. English supplied the judgement.

Three words, one verb, and none of them wearing it on the outside.

One to refuse. An \textbf{usher} looks like a member of this family and is not: the word is built on Latin \emph{ostium}, a \textbf{door}. An usher is a door-keeper.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{usar}. And you can hear the same verb inside three English words that hide it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{usar}
  \item \emph{usar la llave}
  \item \emph{la mano}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{usury} mean before it meant anything harsh? (Payment for the use of money — a use.) What is a \emph{utensil}, taken word for word? (Something that is to be used.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tocar]{tocar — a word that began as a knock}

\label{lesson:ES-C385-tocar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to forget}, then \emph{to use}. (\emph{Olvidar}; \emph{usar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la puerta — something you knock on.
  \item la mesa — something you touch.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to-CAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tocar} — \textquotedblleft{}to touch.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is a Romance verb \textbf{toccare}, and its first meaning was harder than the one it ended with: to \textbf{knock}, to \textbf{strike} — the word you would use for a bell being struck.

Watch the softening. A strike, made lighter and lighter, becomes a tap; a tap, made lighter still, becomes a touch. English \textbf{touch} came out of the same verb through Old French, carrying the same slide with it.

That is also why \emph{tocar} is the Spanish word for making a piano or a guitar sound. Striking a bell and touching a key are the one idea, seen at two pressures.

The Italians kept the older feel in a word English borrowed whole: a \textbf{toccata} is a piece written to show what a player's \emph{touch} can do.

Two cautions, because the shelf around this word is full of look-alikes.

Where \emph{toccare} itself came from is a question the two dictionaries answer at different volumes. The Academy's entry says flatly: \emph{from the sound} \textbf{toc} — the word is an imitation of a knock, full stop. Corominas agrees and adds the reason it convinces him, which is that every Romance language has its own version, as you would expect of a noise rather than an inheritance. The English dictionaries are more cautious and write \emph{perhaps}. Worth noticing that the more confident answer here is the Spanish one; that is not always the way round.

And English \textbf{took} is not a relative. It came from Old Norse, through the Germanic side of English, with no Latin anywhere in it. Nor is a \textbf{toque}, the tall hat. Nor, for that matter, are \textbf{tact} and \textbf{contact}, which are about touching but come from an entirely different Latin verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{tocar}. And you can hear a bell inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tocar}
  \item \emph{tocar la puerta}
  \item \emph{usar y tocar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{toccare} mean before it meant touching? (Knocking or striking, as on a bell.) Is English \emph{took} a relative? (No — it came through Germanic, with no Latin in it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mezclar]{mezclar — the word that was once a brawl}

\label{lesson:ES-C385-mezclar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to use}, then \emph{to touch}. (\emph{Usar}; \emph{tocar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la sal — something you mix in.
  \item el azúcar — something else you mix in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mez-CLAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{z} is a soft \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} across much of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mezclar} — \textquotedblleft{}to mix.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had \textbf{miscere}, to mix. Everyday spoken Latin roughened it into \textbf{misculare} — a form that carries a star, meaning nobody found it written down and it was worked out backwards from the words that came after. It is that spoken form, not the written one, that became \emph{mezclar}, by way of an older Spanish \textbf{mesclar} that the Academy still routes the entry through.

That matters, because the family split there and the two halves came out of it looking nothing alike.

The spoken branch gave English two words, and they are the true siblings of \emph{mezclar}.

\textbf{Meddle} is one. It arrived through French, and its meaning shifted a step at a time: to mix, then to mix oneself in, then to interfere. Somebody who meddles is doing exactly what the word says.

\textbf{Medley} is the better one. Today it means a mixture — a medley of songs. But around the year 1300 a medley was a \textbf{hand-to-hand fight}, a scrum, bodies mixed together. That is the picture the word started from: not a pleasant blend, a pile-up.

The written branch went to the learned words. \textbf{Mixture} comes straight off Latin \emph{mixtus} rather than through the spoken verb. \textbf{Promiscuous} is \emph{pro-} plus \emph{miscere}, mingled without sorting; its narrow modern sense is only about a hundred and fifty years old. \textbf{Miscellaneous} is there too.

Same family, two roads, and the road decides how the word looks.

Spanish keeps a quieter relative of its own. \textbf{Mecer} is the same Latin root, and it now means to rock a cradle — mixing, slowed down to a single gentle motion.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{mezclar}. And you know which English words came by the spoken road.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mezclar}
  \item \emph{mezclar la sal}
  \item \emph{el azúcar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{medley} around 1300? (A hand-to-hand fight.) What is somebody doing, word for word, when they meddle? (Mixing themselves in.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[colgar]{colgar — a couch is a placing}

\label{lesson:ES-C385-colgar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to touch}, then \emph{to mix}. (\emph{Tocar}; \emph{mezclar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la ropa — something you hang.
  \item el armario — where you hang it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{col-GAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, as in \emph{gato}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{colgar} — \textquotedblleft{}to hang.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{collocare} meant to place, to lay, to set something in position. It is \emph{com-} plus \emph{locare}, and \emph{locare} is about a \emph{place}.

English got it as a piece of furniture. Old French turned \emph{collocare} into \emph{couchier}, to lay down, to go to bed — and English borrowed that as \textbf{couch}. A couch is, word for word, a \emph{placing}: the thing you lay yourself down on.

Now the honest part, because this is where a tidy story would lie to you.

English kept the old meaning. \emph{Couch} is about laying something down. Spanish did not: \emph{colgar} means to \textbf{hang}, which is placing something so that it does \emph{not} come to rest.

Nothing on the English side explains that. The shift from placing to hanging happened inside Spanish and only inside Spanish, and the English cousin cannot be used as evidence for it. What English gives you is the \emph{root}, not the meaning — and knowing which of the two a cognate is offering you is most of the skill.

Spanish also kept the plain descendant beside the shifted one: \emph{colocar} still means to place. Two verbs, one Latin ancestor, and centuries of drift between them.

English did the same trick. Beside the worn-down \emph{couch} it also has the tidy Latin \textbf{collocate}, borrowed straight off the page much later. One verb, entering the same language twice, once through a mouth and once through a book.

One to refuse: \textbf{cough} is not in this family. It is Germanic, and made out of the noise.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{colgar}. And you know when a cognate is evidence and when it is only a root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{colgar}
  \item \emph{colgar la ropa}
  \item \emph{el armario}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a couch, taken back to Latin? (A placing — the thing you lay yourself down on.) Which side of the family moved to \textquotedblleft{}hang\textquotedblright{}? (The Spanish side; English kept \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
